video_title: Luis Garicano on Spain, Europe, and the Future of Work
transcript: TYLER COWEN: Hello, everyone, and welcome back to  Conversations with Tyler. Today I am honored to   be speaking with Luis Garicano. He is a Spanish  economist, one of the best-known and also best   economists in Europe. He was also a member of the  European Parliament. He taught at the University   of Chicago Business School. He is now, for the  second time, at London School of Economics.   He has a new and excellent book out, as far as I  know, the best book on AI and the job market. It   is called Messy Jobs, and it is co-authored  with Jin Li and Yanhui Wu. Luis, welcome. LUIS GARICANO: Thanks very much for  having me. It’s really a pleasure. COWEN: We will get to Messy Jobs, but  first I have so many questions about Spain.   Why is it that Spain has become so  NIMBY? Before the Great Financial Crisis,   there’s so many homes being built, right?  There’s overbuilding, everyone goes crazy,   and now it seems to be land of NIMBY. What’s  been the switch in the political equilibrium? GARICANO: There is part of it which is ideas  matter. Spain was pretty permissive about housing.   There was a pretty elastic supply, and people were  building all over the place, up to 800,000 houses   a year, which is a lot for a country. What  happened is that we got a housing bubble. It   exploded. There was a lot of overbuilding at  the time, for many reasons. Basically, there was   a triangle between promoters and  politicians, local politicians,   and the savings banks, a bit like your S&L crisis.  People identified easy building with corruption,   and people identified easy building  with high prices, believe it or not. There really is a serious debate in the Spanish  media. Maybe, I guess, you’re not so surprised   with Mamdami in New York. There is a very serious  debate on whether building more houses would lower   prices. There are people saying that, no, it  has nothing to do with how many houses you have.   People think that building wouldn’t solve it,  and they think that you need to restrict tourist   flats and so on. There has been some of that. There has also been, after the bubble, a big  restriction on the rights of municipalities to   make decisions on land, because it was supposed  to lead to corruption. This is something that has   happened in many areas, that you’re trying  to make people accountable, and you end up   making people scared and unempowering the people  who could make the decisions. You end up with   a completely rigid supply, which is what we have  now, hundreds of thousands of immigrants per year,   only less than 100,000 houses built per year, and  indeed, as you said, no YIMBY movement at all.   It’s completely NIMBY. There is nobody in  Spain—just a very few people, including me—saying,   hey, let’s build more housing. COWEN: If you drive through Spain, which  I’m sure you’ve done more than I have,   a lot of it is really quite empty, right? GARICANO: Completely. COWEN: You see those big billboards with  the black bull and nothing else for miles.   What are you going to do with all that  land? What does that equilibrium look   like? That simply people crowd into a  few cities and the rest just dwindles? GARICANO: Yes, the current way that housing is  built is basically very much by agglomerating in   the center. A very large share, I don’t remember  the exact number, but a very large share of the   densest census tracts in square kilometers in  Europe are in Spain, in Madrid, in Barcelona,   which is surprising for a country that is  completely empty. First, we are putting a lot of   solar energy on that empty land. Second, there  is a lot of restrictions on what you can do with   it because of biodiversity. There’s a ring around  Madrid where you cannot build, like around London. Barcelona, people think you couldn’t build.  People think Barcelona is full. In fact,   all the area around the airport is empty,  and it’s green, it’s agricultural land.   People in Barcelona are convinced it’s  impossible to grow the city. A lot of it   has to do with biodiversity regulations  and an effort to keep nature, and so on.   My other country is England, of course, where  I’m working and living right now. In England,   the United Kingdom has this view that if  you touch any bird, that construction has   to be completely stopped. Spain is not at that  extreme, but all of those concerns matter a lot. COWEN: Why is there a current  productivity crisis in Spain? GARICANO: Productivity indeed hasn’t grown for  three decades, more or less. We’re currently   having extensive growth. We’re having immigration,  we’re having tourism, but we don’t really have   productivity. A lot of it has to do with the  political economy. I think if you want to explain   the West, not just Spain, you have to understand  who is voting and who is this being governed   for. Spain is a particularly low-fertility, high  life-expectancy country. We have the fifth-lowest   fertility and the fifth-highest life expectancy  in the world grosso modo, and very high pensions. Essentially, all the GDP growth we’ve had has  gone, 100 percent of the GDP growth we’ve had   since 2008 has gone to pensions, to  the pensioners. In terms of investment,   there is very little in terms of productive  investment. We have this fantastic highway   network and this high-speed rail network. It’s  not really getting the maintenance it needs. Just   as one example, the country is basically being  governed by and for the older retired people. COWEN: What does the optimistic  scenario look like? You don’t   have to predict it’s going to happen, but  lay out for me how it could all go well.   You would get productivity growth of 1.5 percent a  year, and economic growth a bit higher than that. GARICANO: Spain has amazing fundamentals for the  current situation, meaning we could easily be very   electricity-energy rich due to solar, wind, and  nuclear. We have all this empty space where you   could put nuclear plants without much resistance.  In fact, we are closing them for political   reasons. The energy could be a big advantage. It’s  a really amazing place to live. There is no more   diverse geography and climate and nature  anywhere in Europe, I think, or close to,   and beautiful. You could easily see a  situation where Spain becomes Florida, or   Austin, Texas. Think of  Texas. It attracts technology,   attracts talent who wants to live there,  attracts energy, builds the data centers,   et cetera. That scenario is not impossible.  The political economy is the tricky part. COWEN: Doesn’t that mean you actually don’t have  good fundamentals? You said you don’t even have a   YIMBY movement. Life there really is quite good.  I’ve been many times. It’s one of my favorite   countries to visit. Isn’t that like a resource  curse where there’s no sense of crisis? Old people   live for a long time. It’s very comfortable.  The weather’s great. The food is amazing.   Aren’t those, in fact, liabilities  in a time of very rapid change? GARICANO: I think that’s a great point.  The political economy is the constraint.   We have had reforms in Spain, including during  the dictatorship when the crisis situation was   unsustainable. Spain opened up under American  pressure in ’59 and had the highest growth rate   in the ’60s. It reformed in the mid-’80s and early  ’80s with the socialist government that was very   actually pro-growth and pro-development, a YIMBY  socialist government. Imagine the socialist   government that eliminated housing, rent control,  which right now is coming back everywhere. It reformed, again, coming up to the  euro, although as Tano Santos and   Jesús Fernández-Villaverde have shown in the  Journal of Economic Perspectives article,   that pro-reform movement before the euro was  gone in all Southern Europe once the euro   made the urgency go away. It has reformed again in  2012 under the euro crisis and Spanish crisis. It   could do the reforms it needs. It’s going  to have to be through a crisis, I’m afraid. COWEN: Now, you come from Valladolid,  which as you know, for a long time has   been an automotive center. Should the European  Union impose strict tariffs and quotas on, say,   Chinese electric vehicles, self-driving cars? GARICANO: I don’t have a religious view  on this and other industrial policies. I   think that you have to evaluate them. There  is an article by Dani Rodrik and co-authors,   recent review, which says industrial policies  work under some conditions, not under others.   We know they have worked in Korea at some point,  et cetera. What do they need? They need to be able   to have the conditions to let losers fail, and you  need to have an objective, a clear-cut objective. Now, is Europe in a situation to have an  industrial policy where losers are allowed to fail   in the car industry, and where Europe  has a clear view of where we should go?   I think the answer is no on both. In terms of what  the losers’ power is, basically, any industrial   policy would be governed for and by the losers.  Basically, as we have seen, the traditional car   companies are receiving all the help and all  the aid. Whether we know what the objective is,   we have a melange of conflicting environmental,  labor, industrial security objectives.   I wouldn’t be very optimistic about the chance of  success of an industrial policy on large scale,   tax these cars, try to make these legacy  companies suddenly become cutting edge. I also think that what we are seeing is that  European companies are getting destroyed in   third-world markets. In Latin America, you  only see BYDs now; in Africa, everywhere else.   I don’t think that would solve much. I can see  the short-run pressure, and I understand it.   I think our problems are different. Our problems  are about labor regulations that allow people to   adapt fast, are about lack of innovation, and are  about lack of incentives for radical as opposed to   incremental innovation. Europe is very good  at incremental, little by little innovation.   We’re really not good at making radical  changes. I think that’s where the problem is. COWEN: Let’s say the automotive sector  leaves Valladolid, which is a city of what,   300,000, 400,000 people? It’s not  huge. It would be a major blow.   What would actually replace it? What  would the place look like 10 years later? GARICANO: For Valladolid, it would be  devastating. It would be devastating.   Both Valladolid and Valencia are big centers for  Renault and Michelin, the car tire company and the   car manufacturing brand. It would be devastating.  The other industry that Valladolid has been   the capital of Castile-Lyon. It’s a very  bureaucratic, intensive country. You know   Spain had a bureaucracy before anybody else had a  bureaucracy. I guess China also had a bureaucracy.   That’s the other industry, which is not  a very promising industry. I think that   what we need to do is to give a  chance to innovation and to change.   The way we’re doing it is just slowing  down all change and all adaptation. COWEN: There was a media article  recently. It said something like,   well, Americans don’t read anymore, texts aside,  but the Spanish, they still read. Do you agree?   Books and novels, not on your smartphone. GARICANO: I guess there’s quite a lot of  reading among females, much more than men.   I think it happens, women more than men. I  think it happens everywhere in the world,   meaning that also the publishing  world is adapting to that.   I’m not sure I understand why women are  remaining a more loyal constituency of books.   I don’t know the figures. My sense is that Spain  is going through the same shorter attention span,   TikTok short videos. When you’re in the public  transport and you see what people are doing,   they’re just hitting the videos with the  same finger as everywhere else in the world. COWEN: If I walk into a bookstore in Spain,  I’m struck by how much the front tables   are mostly fiction, and there’s  a relative paucity of nonfiction. GARICANO: That’s correct. COWEN: The US is actually  moving in that direction,   but we used to be very much the other  way around. Why that difference? GARICANO: That’s a great question. There is not  a long tradition of nonfiction. If you think of   what are your remarkable 150 or 200 books from  Spain, none of them will be nonfiction. In fact,   it is also related to the fact that Spain doesn’t  have a big tradition on research and innovation.   Spain has always had a humanistic, artistic—think  of our powers in the 16th, 17th [centuries], best   painters, best writers from Cervantes—I was  thinking Velázquez and Goya as painters,   Cervantes, Calderón, and all the 20th-century  fantastic writers from Lorca, et cetera. If you try to think of, just for example, who is  the last Nobel Prize winner in science from Spain,   you will have to go back to 1905. It’s really a  long time in coming. The culture doesn’t reward   a lot nonfiction, science. It rewards sports  very well, market-driven excellence, big rewards,   big concentration at the top, very  large labor mobility. It rewards   all these artistic expressions, which, by the  way, two things where you won’t see AI encroach,   or AI will encroach much more slowly.  Maybe that’s protecting Spain. COWEN: Other than some obvious  choices, like say Cervantes,   what in Spanish language fiction  is especially meaningful to you? GARICANO: There is a lot of writing from the Latin  American boom that I have enjoyed enormously.   I have enjoyed García Márquez. I have  enjoyed Rodolfo Pedro Páramo. I have enjoyed   Vargas Llosa. I have laughed, I have  cried with Vargas Llosa, who, by the way,   very free market thinker as well, wrote an essay,  a nonfiction collection on liberal thinkers.   I have enjoyed a lot of Latin American writing.  In terms of Spanish writing, the poetry from the   1929 generation—García Lorca, Miguel  Hernández, those people are amazing as well. COWEN: I like Javier Cercas. Do you like him? GARICANO: I love Cercas. He has some really good  mystery novels, which are fantastic, but he also   has this Anatomía de un Instante, this nonfiction  novelized book that I would recommend very   strongly to people to read about the Spanish coup  d’état in 1981. He writes from the perspective of   three main characters, who are three people  coming from the civil war, who were all three   betrayers of their own cause, the communist  leader who actually was in favor of the monarchy,   the secretary general of the party who was  the prime minister, who made the transition,   and the general who was on the Franco side  who made the military accepted transition. Those were the only three people,  coincidentally, who didn’t go under the   desks when the guys, the civil guards  with the guns came storming into the   house, which was in session to vote the  successor of Suárez, the prime minister.   He manages to weave those lives and that story  beautifully. I really recommend that book. COWEN: That’s a great book. I  also like Soldiers of Salamis   and the recent one about the trip with the pope. GARICANO: Yes, he’s all around really fantastic. COWEN: Why is the Spanish civil war still  so focal? I’m thinking of your literature,   but also your politics. Why is that stuck as  such a thing in Spain? It’s a long time ago now. GARICANO: It’s true. It frustrates me very  much, and it frustrates many of us. It probably   is because many people think it wasn’t a really  well-closed episode. It wasn’t an episode where,   if you think of maybe the South Africa  reconciliation, there was an explicit   reconciliation. If you think of the German  dictatorship, there was an actual surrender. Franco died in bed. He started the civil  war. He won the civil war. He installed a   dictatorship, and he then died in bed.  There was no revolution like in Portugal,   that pushed him out. Many people  feel that the transition to democracy   was not a true people-driven transition,  but it was driven by the Franco elites. The truth is there were many people in Spain  at the time, including the communist leader   I mentioned, Carrillo, who thought, never again.  Let’s try to do things now peacefully and well,   and they handled the transition admirably.  I think it’s time to put all that behind us. COWEN: Today, how is it that you understand  the public choice economics of Catalonia? GARICANO: There is a very clear historical  inequality, which is the Basques   had a terrorist movement. Because they had a  terrorist movement, they managed to preserve   a confederal system of financing in the  constitution. They say it's because of historical   reasons. That's BS. When you do the constitution,  you redo the history. You start from scratch.   Because people were scared of this terrorist  movement, they were allowed the following bizarre   exception. Everybody gets financing through the  taxation system, and you get some taxes that go to   your region and some taxes that go to the central  government, except the Basque Country, which   has itself collects all the  taxes and negotiates bilaterally. Imagine Texas negotiating bilaterally  with the US government, how much Texas   is going to contribute to the US budget. Now,  here's the smart thing, or the terrible thing.   They have enough votes to flip government  every few years. They wait for that negotiation   till the moment when they actually can decide  that this government is going to continue,   is going to drop. They do always the negotiation  in that moment, which means that what is called   the cupo, the contribution of the Basque Country  to Spain, is basically frozen. In fact, even   when the pensions go up, the rest of the country  pays them. The Basques don't actually pay more. They actually are net recipients from Spain,  even though they are one of the richest regions.   Catalonia sees this and says, hey, we  want the same system. The problem is,   the Basque Country is small. Catalonia is very  large. It's not sustainable to do a system   like that because it would break the budget if  you have two of the biggest regions bargaining   bilaterally with the state over how much they're  going to contribute every five or 10 years.   That's going to be unsustainable. That's the  reason this basic inequality in the constitution   has created a system that is unstable, and  that doesn't actually have any solution at all. COWEN: What did the University of  Chicago teach you about politics   that Spain ended up proving wrong? GARICANO: I think what I learned  at the University of Chicago   helps very much with understanding politics.  Politicians are pretty smart maximizers.   I guess voters are pretty inattentive. I  think that your colleague, Bryan Caplan,   wrote a beautiful book about it, The Myth of the  Rational Voter, which is perfectly rational that   they are inattentive. If we doubt why do they  have the incentive to stand up and vote, why   would they have the incentive to figure out what  the program of the different parties is? They’re   inattentive. I think that that’s not clear enough  from the rational models of political economy. The thing that I think I understood when I was  actually doing politics better than I understood   before, and I actually wrote a paper about  it, is the importance of the party discipline.   The mechanism that connects the voters to the  politicians is very weak because we have in many   countries in Europe, even in other countries,  happens through other means like in the UK, but   we don’t need to discuss that, but that mechanism  that connects the voters and the parties is a   mechanism that is mediated. Sorry, the voters and  the law is mediated by internal party discipline. The parties don’t look for the smartest person  for the job or the most competent person for   the job or the person who can design the  right policy. They actually want people   who owe their position to the party so they won’t  complain. It’s not the one who in the town hall   votes more smartly or proposes the smartest things  who gets to the next layer of the proportional   representation system. It’s the one who’s  been most subordinate to the party decisions. That’s why the Socialist Party, which is now in  enormous corruption scandals, unprecedented in   all directions, there is nobody in the party, and  definitely nobody in the Congress supportive of   Prime Minister Sánchez, who is actually making any  noise because their alternative option is zero.   The parties look for people whose outside option  is zero in order to make sure that they keep the   control. That’s, I think, completely rational,  and it would have been predicted by any Chicago   economist on the basis of the incentives, but  it’s not something that I was as aware of. For example, how do parties in Europe choose  the president of the European Commission? Do   they choose the smartest person that  is going to make the best calls? No.   The leaders of the different countries, they  actually want to keep the power. They don’t want   somebody in Brussels who is kind of shallowing  them. They look for somebody who won’t give them   any trouble. We’ve had two Luxembourg people,  one failed defense minister from Germany who is   the current president. We have people who are  just not able to lead, and that is by design. I think that part of how the party  machines and the insight of the way   that this promotion, adverse election, you could  say, this promotion to higher office gets done,   was something that I didn’t understand well  before politics, I think, not sufficiently well. COWEN: You’ve served in the  European Parliament. Should   the EU keep its unanimity  rule for major decisions? GARICANO: The EU has majority rule in  single-market decisions and unanimity rules   in things that fall out of its core, meaning  taxes, defense, foreign policy; in a sense,   you could say all the core functions of the state.  The states don’t want to lose decisions here. Let me give you an example. Armament procurement.  You would say, “Hey, guys, you’re making multiple   tanks. You spend many times more in defense  than Russia. Just make one tank, make one plane,   and one cannon.” What happens? Well, let’s say  that Germany wants to export to Israel. France   doesn’t want that, let’s say, or Spain  doesn’t want that. Germany doesn’t want   Spain and France to make a coalition and  veto it, and vice versa. What happens is   the countries want to have the ultimate right to  decide on all defense matters. That means that you   get multiple procurement decisions, incompatible  shells in the cannons, all of these things. Now, should we have it? Yes. Should we have  the majority vote that you proposed? Yes.   Should we understand the politics that  make it very hard? Those politics are   the core of the state sovereignty, which is  taxation, defense, foreign affairs, all this.   The functions that the state of 1600 or  1700 had originally are all not in Europe.   The politics make it very hard. I told you  defense, but I could go through many other   examples and show you why even though you would  want to think that the gains from a single market,   single procurement, et cetera, would be  enormous, the politics make it really hard. Right now, what we’re doing is harmonizing the  shells. You have a big meeting group. People,   they say, “Oh, I want the 55 millimeters  to be like this.” Somebody says, “No,   I want it like this, 55 1/2.” They meet  for weeks and weeks and weeks and weeks   and come up with pages and pages. People, the  citizens are upset. The truth of the matter is   there is a political reason for  this, and it’s the one I mentioned. So fiscal—Ireland wants to do a separate  tax in Luxembourg, separate tax policy   that basically attracts multinationals and  lowers the tax base and all of those things.   The rest would want no arbitration tax basis. This  is by unanimity. As long as there’s one loser,   no change takes place. In all of these  policies, there’s always one loser.   Pareto improvements are the  only ones that can happen. COWEN: You have your finger on a button, and you  can press the button, and the unanimity rule goes   away, and it’s replaced by two-thirds  majority rule. Do you press the button? GARICANO: Everything. Not  even the US has that, right? COWEN: Correct. GARICANO: Not even the US. Let’s say Europe gets  the same commerce clause as the US. Let me put it   like this. On the function that the US government  has, Europe loses unanimity, I would say yes. COWEN: Could a euro bond work at a  significant level under current institutions? GARICANO: No. You cannot have the four housemates  of the apartment share the credit card bill   without sharing anything about how the money  is spent and how the money is raised. Then   the incentives are for all the housemates to go  around with the common credit card and spend it. I’ve been a very big proponent, and I was a  proponent of the recovery and reconstruction   fund for Europe. We proposed it together with some  revenue functions for Europe that would allow for   the Hamiltonian compromise. The money  gets centralized for some public goods   that are European public goods, and you raise  it in some European way. That has not happened.   We issued those bonds, which we do have, so euro  bonds do exist, without really any joint revenue. COWEN: Capital markets seem to be a big problem.   What could we do to make EU capital  markets stronger and better? GARICANO: It’s very interesting because I wrote  about this in Silicon Continent, in my Substack,   a piece with Per Strömberg. Sweden  has enough money to fund startups   and scale those startups up. Per Strömberg is one  of the biggest world experts on private equity,   and he happens to be also an expert in Sweden  because he’s based in the Stockholm School.   The basic story that he tells, and that I wanted  to write in a blog for our readers with him,   is that it is not really about having the cash.  It’s about the cash and the knowledge together. The money exists. Europe sends the money to the  US. We invest in all those startups. The talent   exists; all those French and Germans in Anthropic  and all these other places. What is missing is   the Spotify chief of marketing that actually  has seen how companies run, how it’s scaled,   et cetera, and now has a lot of money, and starts  to fund startups, advise them, and help them. It’s possible that it is true our capital markets  are a problem, but it is possible that just   fixing the other aspects, which is at the national  level allowing for the big change that Sweden did,   is that you don’t pay those taxes on the capital  gains as long as they are reinvested in the new   startups. Then you create this ball that starts  rolling in which all these startup funders start   funding the new startups. You can do it in a  country that was supposed to be one of the most   socialist in Europe. In fact, it’s a very  free market thanks to internal reform. It’s true the capital markets are not working.  It’s also true the capital market changes we’re   doing are wrong. The main thing I learned about  Europe in that respect is when we do efforts,   instead of we put this new law and eliminate  the previous ones, the way it often happens   in the European Parliament, European Commission,  European Council, the European institutions, is   we add this new law which is harmonized,  but leave all the lower-layer laws there. For example, we are giving right now in  the new capital markets package more power   to the European Securities Markets Authority,  the ESMA, the SEC at the European level,   without removing any power from the  SEC at the national level, which means   you’re not harmonizing anything. You’re just  having more hurdles for people to raise money. COWEN: You mentioned your Substack,  Silicon Continent. I’m happy to recommend   that strongly as well. Now, in labor  markets, should severance protection   rise with the tenure of the worker, or  why not just let the market handle that? GARICANO: I have written and argued  in favor of more flexible markets.   Denmark has found a solution that I think  achieves both ends in protecting workers by   having relatively or pretty high unemployment  insurance, but in making it flexible and able   to hire and fire. That would be, to me, the best  solution to the current rigidity on European labor   markets. The problem is that it costs quite a  bit of money because you have to insure people   quite significantly to make  them be happy to move around. There are solutions in Northern Europe  that allow for this flexicurity, and   I would wish that the rest of Europe was adopting  them because I do believe that it’s not just that   rigid labor markets raise the cost for companies.  You can then lower wages and neutralize it.   The problem is they increase, hugely,  the cost of making mistakes. That’s what   a new literature is recognizing.  People weren’t clear about that before. If Facebook makes a mistake, thinks the future is  the metaverse, and the metaverse is a completely   ridiculous idea, and the future is AI, Facebook  can turn on a dime, fire all the engineers in   metaverse, and hire all the ones in AI in a week.  If Ericsson or Nokia want to do something similar,   they’re going to take months and months and months  of negotiation with their labor council and so on   to the point that they might  go under in the meantime. COWEN: Before we get to your new book, Messy Jobs,   are you game for a round of  overrated versus underrated? GARICANO: Sure. Go ahead. COWEN: Okay. Rosalía—overrated or underrated? GARICANO: Rated just fine. She’s amazing. COWEN: Penelope Cruz. GARICANO: Also fine. A very  fine actress doing very well. COWEN: Javier Marías, the author. GARICANO: I am a big fan. I would say he deserves  wider recognition, so I would say underrated. COWEN: The Spanish painter Antonio Saura. GARICANO: Just fine. Let me just say just fine. COWEN: I think he’s underrated  outside of Spain, for instance. GARICANO: Yes, he is big in Spain,   but I wouldn’t be able to comment on  how internationally he’s recognized. COWEN: The region of Spain,  Extremadura, overrated or underrated? GARICANO: Underrated. It has some  of the best history. Many of the   conquistadors came from there. So when  they went back, they did a lot of work in   making the cities beautiful. The region stopped  growing 400 years ago, so it’s all frozen   in time, and you have some of the most stunning  experiences of walking into a portal toward the   past in places like Cáceres, which, by the way,  has one of the best restaurants in Spain as well. COWEN: What’s it called? GARICANO: The restaurant in Cáceres,   I don’t remember. I ate there a few months  ago. It’s a three-star. I don't remember. COWEN: The AI's will know. Within  the world of Beatle fandom,   is the album Sergeant Pepper  overrated or underrated? GARICANO: I think it’s overrated. I’m not as huge  a fan of that as of Abbey Road or of Rubber Soul   or, for sure, the earlier ones. I don’t  think it’s the biggest piece in the canon. COWEN: There are some weak songs on it. I  think the George Harrison contribution is   not so wonderful. “When I’m Sixty-Four”  is charming, but it bores me a bit. GARICANO: Yes, I think there is some  weakness. I would agree with you. COWEN: Is there an underrated Beatles album?  Again, this is within the world of Beatle fandom. GARICANO: People somehow don’t  like Let It Be, which I think   the post not quite last album, but the really  last album. I don’t know why. I always adored it.   It’s so relative. Their albums  are all hugely appreciated. COWEN: What is the special food place  in Spain that not everyone knows about? GARICANO: The place where I’m sitting now, I’m in  Asturias, recording this from Asturias. It’s the   region in the north between Galicia and Cantabria  in the Basque country. It’s the oldest bit of   Spain in many ways because it was the last place  to be conquered by the Islamic invasion in 711.   It’s where the Reconquista started. Historically,  it has a long history of Romanic churches and all   that, but it also has outstanding food everywhere,  wherever you stop. It has amazing nature,   unspoiled, beautiful beaches, and it’s completely  climate change proof. It has amazing weather. COWEN: How will the Spanish language change? GARICANO: The way it’s changing  is it’s incorporating a lot of   English language words and expressions.  Probably I am guilty of that as well.   People who are very exposed to English introduce  expressions and false friends. We are so careful   not to introduce false friends from Spanish  into English, and then somehow they come back   from English into Spanish, and you see words that  are used. If you are English speaker, you realize,   “Oh, that’s completely the English usage.” That’s  the biggest word. Many words that are ambiguous,   instead of shifting toward the Spanish  use, they shift toward the English one. COWEN: If I’m in Latin America, I notice  that the conditional and subjunctive are   used much less often than in Spain. Given that  Madrid now is, what, 20 percent Latin American,   is this going to affect Spanish in Spain? GARICANO: That’s a great point. We are getting a  very big Latin American influx. I haven’t noticed   that. I haven’t noticed the change in the use  of subjunctive. We use, unlike the French,   not just the subjunctive present. I don’t want  to discourage our listeners from learning, but   we use a lot the compound past subjunctive. If  you make a future statement that is hypothetical,   the hypothetical future is subjunctive.  If I were a rich man—past subjunctive.   I haven’t noticed people using it less, or  at least not among people I hear regularly. COWEN: In Mexico, at least nonlearned people,  they don’t use the future tense very much.   They’ll use the present tense and  maybe throw in the word mañana,   or it’ll depend on context. Spanish in  Spain, is it going to go that way as well? GARICANO: I haven’t noticed  those changes in Spain.   I think that the impact of English language  is orders of magnitude higher than Latin   America. That’s my sense, but I would have to  consult my favorite LLM before being so sure. COWEN: On Messy Jobs, your new and excellent book,   you argue very persuasively, “In my  view, AI will not lead to anything like   mass unemployment, maybe not even to a rise in  unemployment, because jobs will become messier   and the AIs won’t be able to do them.” Is that  a fair description of part of your argument? GARICANO: I think that’s completely right. Yes. COWEN: Now, I agree with you, but I think my worry  is the opposite, that I know a lot of people,   they want simple jobs, they’re  okay with some measure of tedium,   and that if most jobs become messy jobs,   for them, that’s quite stressful, and they’re  upset and disoriented. Do you worry about that? GARICANO: I think that we will have to have  a tolerance for human relations. Is that what   your friends don’t want? We have a tolerance for  relational work that is complex, that has politics   in it, that has a big human component, and  that’s the part that is going to stay. If people   just want to be in their desk typing away, I  think two good ways to think about it is work   from home and outsourcing. If you think of which  jobs were offshored, let me say offshored, in the   big offshoring wave to India, those are jobs  that are not messy. They’re clean. The company   specifies the jobs. They say, “Okay, we can  specify this job perfectly. Let’s ship you up.” Those jobs are the same exact  ones that are under complete   threat of disruption. A lot of the work from home,   when it doesn’t involve a lot of submittings,  I guess, has the same feature. Those jobs are   clean, single-task, and very often verifiable.  You can just see how the performance is going   and have your RL, your reinforcement learning  loop work on those. I think those are gone. The messy component that I want to  emphasize, many people will say, “Oh,   AI will tend to the messiness as well.” I think  that there is some messiness that is contingent   and that AI can streamline, but there is a lot of  messiness that is both relational and has to do   with a deeper aspect of the knowledge problem  that doesn’t really go away. As AI advances,   many aspects of Hayek, Polanyi, and all  these knowledge problems are still there. COWEN: How much retraining will be required  and how frequent will that retraining have   to be? If I think of me working with agents,  I have to retrain myself every month or two.   That’s difficult for me. It’s not stressful  given my position, but I can imagine it   would be stressful. Can we really just put  a big chunk of the labor force through that? GARICANO: Raffaella Sadun and others at  HBS have been working on this. One of   the things that is frustrating about retraining  programs, and not just retraining individuals,   but retraining programs, is that  they generally don’t work.   The favorite middle-of-the-road free market  economist prescription for technological change is   let’s retrain people. We find that this is really,  really hard to do. Say you wanted to retrain   a clinician, a doctor who’s  learned to diagnose illnesses,   and that suddenly gets very easy—this  is not one of our examples, but just to   give an example—to become a plumber. It’s  not that you couldn’t retrain him because   the plumbing skills are so hard, which they  probably are, to be honest, but not just that, but   because there’s a lot of social identity and other  aspects that are tied to the kind of job you do. Retraining is a huge barrier. The way we retrain  ourselves, as Kuhn said, talking about scientists,   is by dying, and the new generations do new  things. I share your concern about how easy   it will be to get people to learn new tricks. On  the other hand, my Ma is 84 years old, and she   talks to ChatGPT all the time. She has good, long  conversations. I’ve updated it so that she now has   the better version that you can talk over it  and argue back, the very recent improvements. The LLMs are becoming better at eliminating  all the prompting skill and all the skill   that went into making agents, et  cetera. It seems like it’s easier   to use. I think the hardest thing about  LLMs—maybe that’s easier to retrain—the   hardest skill about LLMs is knowing what they can  do. Most people have no idea what you could do   with your AI. That’s the part where a short  focus lesson to a relationship manager at a bank,   where you tell him, here’s the case, you’re going  to visit your client, here are the six questions   you should ask—I’m doing some work with a big  bank on this exact topic, a big experiment—here   are the questions that you could ask before you  have the client meeting, maybe that retraining is   easier on the use case as opposed to retraining  for new jobs, which I think is very hard. COWEN: Do you think the natural  rate of unemployment will go up?   I don’t mean cyclical, but  just due to search, retraining? GARICANO: My sense is that we have several hundred  years of automation, and we do have moments of   blips, but I think the natural rate is going  up much more due to other things. Well,   if you allow me to group participationing, which  has to do with disability and mental illness   and people not feeling well and all that, rather  than to a permanent increase in retraining needs. COWEN: We have some degree of recursive  self-improvement right now. Arguably,   there’s more to come. There’s a new model  out every month or two. For the most part,   they’re much better than the model that existed a  month or two earlier. Just how exactly are people   supposed to keep up with that? Do the jobs  get messier at an equivalently rapid pace? GARICANO: You lose certain bits of the job.  Certain things get unbundled. Other things don’t   get unbundled. Jin and Yanhui and me talk about  strong bundles and weak bundles. Weak bundles,   the job breaks into pieces, and some parts are  done by the AI. When the job is a strong bundle,   the AI comes into your bundle and helps  you, like in a relationship manager,   an account manager for a bank who  gets to prepare the meetings better,   but still needs to have the cognitive  task bundled with seeing the clients. I think that part doesn’t quite require staying as  close to the frontier as you and me are staying.   I think that part requires knowing that the  LLM can help you prepare the client meeting.   You ask the LLM, “Please help me prepare this  client meeting. Here are the budgets and the   balance sheet statements of the client. Help me  see which products of the bank I could offer.”   I don’t think that needs really to  know what the actual frontier model   is and how does it differ from the previous ones. COWEN: Now, as you well know, virtually all  new technologies and productivity improvements,   they lead to more leisure over time in a good  way. I don’t mean unemployment, but actual   enjoyed leisure. If I think of the current day,  there’s some people, like the two of us, we choose   to work more to learn about AI. Then there’s  other people; they feel they have to work more   to learn about AI to not lose their jobs.  So far, there’s no leisure dividend. People   basically are working more. When is  the leisure dividend going to arrive? GARICANO: I’m not sure that’s the case.  Let me give you two data points. One is   a Chinese CEO I had dinner with. My two  co-authors from Hong Kong University   and I, we had dinner with this CEO who told us she  sees every one of her IT people more productive.   She looks at the productivity of the overall  IT department, nothing happens. She said to us,   “I think they are smoking the  productivity gains in the corridor.” The second is from the recent NBER Summer  Institute. There was a paper in health   which gave doctors scribes and they all adopted.  Adoption is slow. Well, the automated scribes   went up to 100 percent of adoption really very  quickly. You see doctors scheduling more meetings   and doing more stuff. Eventually, and there was  a recent New York Times article from a doctor   exactly arguing this. She was saying, “I have more  time for my yoga classes.” She was actually using   the scribe which transcribes the meetings and  which stops a lot of the bureaucratic work that is   nasty for a doctor. My wife is one,  so I know how much they hate that.   She was actually doing more yoga. This  actually shows up in this paper to some extent. I do think that what we see with this  usage, this shadow usage of AI in the job,   which is people have their own  computer, and they actually ask   questions that maybe their corporate AI  doesn’t allow them to ask, has a lot of   welfare gains in the form of leisure and lower  work stress in the job because you just ask the   LLM, you post it there, and you just spend some  time browsing the web. I am not as sure that   the leisure is not expanding, but definitely not  mine. I’ve never worked as much as grad school. COWEN: Say in the short run when taxes change,  almost always the substitution effect overwhelms   the income effect. Tax cut, people work more.  If taxes go up, people work less. Of course,   we see this in Western Europe. Aren’t these AI  productivity improvements a bit like tax changes?   You’re more productive. In the aggregate, if  doctors are more productive, they can earn more;   they’ll work harder. I’m not  complaining about that fact,   but maybe we should expect that  instead of a leisure dividend. GARICANO: Both things can happen. We are seeing  Jevons effects in many of our own utilities and in   many of our own decisions to work. It’s definitely  the case for you and I, as you said. Just   for the amusement of our readers, I guess, many of  you have a WHOOP. I was really very happy with my   WHOOP until January this year. I was 53 years old  in physical age. Since January, it’s been steadily   declining. I’m now 57. I grew four years in six  months. That’s because I am not sleeping a lot. I   am running things into the night and going to bed  thinking, “Oh, I should have done this old thing.   Why didn’t I try this?” Yes, it definitely happens  to me, so why wouldn’t it happen to those doctors? COWEN: Is there a plausible scenario whereby  Spain in particular, and I don’t mean the EU,   I mean Spain, achieves AI sovereignty?  You’ve written about this on your Substack,   Silicon Continent. What’s your view right now?   Keep in mind, the whole stack in some  way has to be under your control, right? GARICANO: Yes, I don’t think that’s a substantive  objective, neither for Spain, nor for Europe.   Europe as a whole, and Spain  in particular, are nowhere on   hardware, except for ASML, which does the  capital equipment. I’ll go back to ASML,   the producer of the machines that make the EUV  chips. We are nowhere on the language models,   the frontier models, neither in open weights,  nor on closed models. We have Mistral,   but it’s not really at the level of the Chinese  ones. We are not really there on the data centers. All the elements that are needed  are not there, except for ASML,   which is a Dutch company and is not under European  jurisdiction, Dutch jurisdiction, if you want.   Much of the supply chain is  German. What you can aspire to,   I’ve been defending the second-mover strategy  for Europe with my colleague Jesús Saa-Requejo.   What we are defending is being a fast implementer,  profiting from the gigantic investment that the   Americans are making in many things that will  actually, like the railroads, eventually not lead   to significant value capture, but will generate  enormous dissipated welfare gains for everybody. Let’s be the ones who enjoy those welfare  gains by adopting AI very aggressively,   becoming big clients. When you’re a big  client, like China showed with Nvidia,   you have bargaining power because the  people who sell to you, your vendors,   are going to lobby the government to keep selling  to you. Become a second mover. Try to make sure to   have options. Keep it interoperable. Make  sure the models can easily be switched,   which at the moment is very, very easy. You  just need to change the API call, and it becomes   seamless. That’s the best that we can do. I don’t  think sovereignty is an objective at this moment. COWEN: How much bargaining power  does Spain lose in this new world? GARICANO: All countries, except the  US and China, will be dependent on AI,   which they don’t control. My view is that, and  I’ve disagreed with my blog co-author and son,   Pieter, on this—this is the one point on which we  disagree. He’s very convinced that it’s all about   frontier models and he’s written a couple of posts  on that. I think that you need frontier models   in research and innovation. You need frontier  models in some adversary applications like war. In order to have good law, good  professional services, good medicine,   good accounting, good companies doing  proprietary research in their own servers,   you don’t need a frontier model. You can be three,  four months behind the frontier as long as you   have the harness in-house, the data in-house.  You’re better off without and I think that   this letter from very recently that Nvidia CEO and  Microsoft CEO stimulated and everybody else wrote   goes in this direction. The open  weights model allows you to keep   proprietary your own data and your own know-how.  A country like Spain, or Europe as a whole, could   build a strategy on that ability to switch and  to keep the market competitive and contestable. COWEN: Let’s say you were liberated  from your AI learning responsibilities   and given two or three free  weeks in life, all expenses paid,   to explore some corner of the world where  you’ve never been. What’s your choice and why? GARICANO: I think I’ll go to Vietnam. It’s one of  the places I’ve been dreaming of going for a long   time. I think it has the cuisine, the landscapes,  the people, the economic side, the technology to   see how they’re doing all this transition,  the nature. I think it would be Vietnam. COWEN: Final question. What is it you want  to learn about next, other than Vietnam? GARICANO: I am continuously fascinated by  economics. I learned a lot of price theory   in Chicago from Becker and Murphy and Rosen, and  those were my advisers and many others. I find   that these tools are allowing me to learn much  more and to be deeper on many questions and to   think harder about what is it that remains messy?  What is the knowledge problem once cognition is   very cheap, and why is it hard to reproduce with  the machine? All of those questions are infinitely   interesting. I spent quite a few years outside  of economics because of the politics detour. Of course, I was in charge of economic dossiers  in parliament, but I was not in the frontier of   economics. I realized how much I like it.  My desire is to learn more about economics   and help the economics discipline and the  students make this beautiful transition   that we’re going to see that suddenly it’s going  to accelerate all sorts of interesting research. COWEN: Luis Garicano, thank you very much. GARICANO: All right. Thank  you, Tyler. It was my pleasure.

transcript_segments.text: TYLER COWEN: Hello, everyone, and welcome back to  Conversations with Tyler. Today I am honored to
be speaking with Luis Garicano. He is a Spanish  economist, one of the best-known and also best
economists in Europe. He was also a member of the  European Parliament. He taught at the University
of Chicago Business School. He is now, for the  second time, at London School of Economics.
He has a new and excellent book out, as far as I  know, the best book on AI and the job market. It
is called Messy Jobs, and it is co-authored  with Jin Li and Yanhui Wu. Luis, welcome.
LUIS GARICANO: Thanks very much for  having me. It’s really a pleasure.
COWEN: We will get to Messy Jobs, but  first I have so many questions about Spain.
Why is it that Spain has become so  NIMBY? Before the Great Financial Crisis,
there’s so many homes being built, right?  There’s overbuilding, everyone goes crazy,
and now it seems to be land of NIMBY. What’s  been the switch in the political equilibrium?
GARICANO: There is part of it which is ideas  matter. Spain was pretty permissive about housing.
There was a pretty elastic supply, and people were  building all over the place, up to 800,000 houses
a year, which is a lot for a country. What  happened is that we got a housing bubble. It
exploded. There was a lot of overbuilding at  the time, for many reasons. Basically, there was
a triangle between promoters and  politicians, local politicians,
and the savings banks, a bit like your S&L crisis.  People identified easy building with corruption,
and people identified easy building  with high prices, believe it or not.
There really is a serious debate in the Spanish  media. Maybe, I guess, you’re not so surprised
with Mamdami in New York. There is a very serious  debate on whether building more houses would lower
prices. There are people saying that, no, it  has nothing to do with how many houses you have.
People think that building wouldn’t solve it,  and they think that you need to restrict tourist
flats and so on. There has been some of that.
There has also been, after the bubble, a big  restriction on the rights of municipalities to
make decisions on land, because it was supposed  to lead to corruption. This is something that has
happened in many areas, that you’re trying  to make people accountable, and you end up
making people scared and unempowering the people  who could make the decisions. You end up with
a completely rigid supply, which is what we have  now, hundreds of thousands of immigrants per year,
only less than 100,000 houses built per year, and  indeed, as you said, no YIMBY movement at all.
It’s completely NIMBY. There is nobody in  Spain—just a very few people, including me—saying,
hey, let’s build more housing.
COWEN: If you drive through Spain, which  I’m sure you’ve done more than I have,
a lot of it is really quite empty, right?
GARICANO: Completely.
COWEN: You see those big billboards with  the black bull and nothing else for miles.
What are you going to do with all that  land? What does that equilibrium look
like? That simply people crowd into a  few cities and the rest just dwindles?
GARICANO: Yes, the current way that housing is  built is basically very much by agglomerating in
the center. A very large share, I don’t remember  the exact number, but a very large share of the
densest census tracts in square kilometers in  Europe are in Spain, in Madrid, in Barcelona,
which is surprising for a country that is  completely empty. First, we are putting a lot of
solar energy on that empty land. Second, there  is a lot of restrictions on what you can do with
it because of biodiversity. There’s a ring around  Madrid where you cannot build, like around London.
Barcelona, people think you couldn’t build.  People think Barcelona is full. In fact,
all the area around the airport is empty,  and it’s green, it’s agricultural land.
People in Barcelona are convinced it’s  impossible to grow the city. A lot of it
has to do with biodiversity regulations  and an effort to keep nature, and so on.
My other country is England, of course, where  I’m working and living right now. In England,
the United Kingdom has this view that if  you touch any bird, that construction has
to be completely stopped. Spain is not at that  extreme, but all of those concerns matter a lot.
COWEN: Why is there a current  productivity crisis in Spain?
GARICANO: Productivity indeed hasn’t grown for  three decades, more or less. We’re currently
having extensive growth. We’re having immigration,  we’re having tourism, but we don’t really have
productivity. A lot of it has to do with the  political economy. I think if you want to explain
the West, not just Spain, you have to understand  who is voting and who is this being governed
for. Spain is a particularly low-fertility, high  life-expectancy country. We have the fifth-lowest
fertility and the fifth-highest life expectancy  in the world grosso modo, and very high pensions.
Essentially, all the GDP growth we’ve had has  gone, 100 percent of the GDP growth we’ve had
since 2008 has gone to pensions, to  the pensioners. In terms of investment,
there is very little in terms of productive  investment. We have this fantastic highway
network and this high-speed rail network. It’s  not really getting the maintenance it needs. Just
as one example, the country is basically being  governed by and for the older retired people.
COWEN: What does the optimistic  scenario look like? You don’t
have to predict it’s going to happen, but  lay out for me how it could all go well.
You would get productivity growth of 1.5 percent a  year, and economic growth a bit higher than that.
GARICANO: Spain has amazing fundamentals for the  current situation, meaning we could easily be very
electricity-energy rich due to solar, wind, and  nuclear. We have all this empty space where you
could put nuclear plants without much resistance.  In fact, we are closing them for political
reasons. The energy could be a big advantage. It’s  a really amazing place to live. There is no more
diverse geography and climate and nature  anywhere in Europe, I think, or close to,
and beautiful. You could easily see a  situation where Spain becomes Florida, or
Austin, Texas. Think of  Texas. It attracts technology,
attracts talent who wants to live there,  attracts energy, builds the data centers,
et cetera. That scenario is not impossible.  The political economy is the tricky part.
COWEN: Doesn’t that mean you actually don’t have  good fundamentals? You said you don’t even have a
YIMBY movement. Life there really is quite good.  I’ve been many times. It’s one of my favorite
countries to visit. Isn’t that like a resource  curse where there’s no sense of crisis? Old people
live for a long time. It’s very comfortable.  The weather’s great. The food is amazing.
Aren’t those, in fact, liabilities  in a time of very rapid change?
GARICANO: I think that’s a great point.  The political economy is the constraint.
We have had reforms in Spain, including during  the dictatorship when the crisis situation was
unsustainable. Spain opened up under American  pressure in ’59 and had the highest growth rate
in the ’60s. It reformed in the mid-’80s and early  ’80s with the socialist government that was very
actually pro-growth and pro-development, a YIMBY  socialist government. Imagine the socialist
government that eliminated housing, rent control,  which right now is coming back everywhere.
It reformed, again, coming up to the  euro, although as Tano Santos and
Jesús Fernández-Villaverde have shown in the  Journal of Economic Perspectives article,
that pro-reform movement before the euro was  gone in all Southern Europe once the euro
made the urgency go away. It has reformed again in  2012 under the euro crisis and Spanish crisis. It
could do the reforms it needs. It’s going  to have to be through a crisis, I’m afraid.
COWEN: Now, you come from Valladolid,  which as you know, for a long time has
been an automotive center. Should the European  Union impose strict tariffs and quotas on, say,
Chinese electric vehicles, self-driving cars?
GARICANO: I don’t have a religious view  on this and other industrial policies. I
think that you have to evaluate them. There  is an article by Dani Rodrik and co-authors,
recent review, which says industrial policies  work under some conditions, not under others.
We know they have worked in Korea at some point,  et cetera. What do they need? They need to be able
to have the conditions to let losers fail, and you  need to have an objective, a clear-cut objective.
Now, is Europe in a situation to have an  industrial policy where losers are allowed to fail
in the car industry, and where Europe  has a clear view of where we should go?
I think the answer is no on both. In terms of what  the losers’ power is, basically, any industrial
policy would be governed for and by the losers.  Basically, as we have seen, the traditional car
companies are receiving all the help and all  the aid. Whether we know what the objective is,
we have a melange of conflicting environmental,  labor, industrial security objectives.
I wouldn’t be very optimistic about the chance of  success of an industrial policy on large scale,
tax these cars, try to make these legacy  companies suddenly become cutting edge.
I also think that what we are seeing is that  European companies are getting destroyed in
third-world markets. In Latin America, you  only see BYDs now; in Africa, everywhere else.
I don’t think that would solve much. I can see  the short-run pressure, and I understand it.
I think our problems are different. Our problems  are about labor regulations that allow people to
adapt fast, are about lack of innovation, and are  about lack of incentives for radical as opposed to
incremental innovation. Europe is very good  at incremental, little by little innovation.
We’re really not good at making radical  changes. I think that’s where the problem is.
COWEN: Let’s say the automotive sector  leaves Valladolid, which is a city of what,
300,000, 400,000 people? It’s not  huge. It would be a major blow.
What would actually replace it? What  would the place look like 10 years later?
GARICANO: For Valladolid, it would be  devastating. It would be devastating.
Both Valladolid and Valencia are big centers for  Renault and Michelin, the car tire company and the
car manufacturing brand. It would be devastating.  The other industry that Valladolid has been
the capital of Castile-Lyon. It’s a very  bureaucratic, intensive country. You know
Spain had a bureaucracy before anybody else had a  bureaucracy. I guess China also had a bureaucracy.
That’s the other industry, which is not  a very promising industry. I think that
what we need to do is to give a  chance to innovation and to change.
The way we’re doing it is just slowing  down all change and all adaptation.
COWEN: There was a media article  recently. It said something like,
well, Americans don’t read anymore, texts aside,  but the Spanish, they still read. Do you agree?
Books and novels, not on your smartphone.
GARICANO: I guess there’s quite a lot of  reading among females, much more than men.
I think it happens, women more than men. I  think it happens everywhere in the world,
meaning that also the publishing  world is adapting to that.
I’m not sure I understand why women are  remaining a more loyal constituency of books.
I don’t know the figures. My sense is that Spain  is going through the same shorter attention span,
TikTok short videos. When you’re in the public  transport and you see what people are doing,
they’re just hitting the videos with the  same finger as everywhere else in the world.
COWEN: If I walk into a bookstore in Spain,  I’m struck by how much the front tables
are mostly fiction, and there’s  a relative paucity of nonfiction.
GARICANO: That’s correct.
COWEN: The US is actually  moving in that direction,
but we used to be very much the other  way around. Why that difference?
GARICANO: That’s a great question. There is not  a long tradition of nonfiction. If you think of
what are your remarkable 150 or 200 books from  Spain, none of them will be nonfiction. In fact,
it is also related to the fact that Spain doesn’t  have a big tradition on research and innovation.
Spain has always had a humanistic, artistic—think  of our powers in the 16th, 17th [centuries], best
painters, best writers from Cervantes—I was  thinking Velázquez and Goya as painters,
Cervantes, Calderón, and all the 20th-century  fantastic writers from Lorca, et cetera.
If you try to think of, just for example, who is  the last Nobel Prize winner in science from Spain,
you will have to go back to 1905. It’s really a  long time in coming. The culture doesn’t reward
a lot nonfiction, science. It rewards sports  very well, market-driven excellence, big rewards,
big concentration at the top, very  large labor mobility. It rewards
all these artistic expressions, which, by the  way, two things where you won’t see AI encroach,
or AI will encroach much more slowly.  Maybe that’s protecting Spain.
COWEN: Other than some obvious  choices, like say Cervantes,
what in Spanish language fiction  is especially meaningful to you?
GARICANO: There is a lot of writing from the Latin  American boom that I have enjoyed enormously.
I have enjoyed García Márquez. I have  enjoyed Rodolfo Pedro Páramo. I have enjoyed
Vargas Llosa. I have laughed, I have  cried with Vargas Llosa, who, by the way,
very free market thinker as well, wrote an essay,  a nonfiction collection on liberal thinkers.
I have enjoyed a lot of Latin American writing.  In terms of Spanish writing, the poetry from the

GARICANO: It’s true. It frustrates me very  much, and it frustrates many of us. It probably

COWEN: Today, how is it that you understand  the public choice economics of Catalonia?
GARICANO: There is a very clear historical  inequality, which is the Basques
had a terrorist movement. Because they had a  terrorist movement, they managed to preserve
a confederal system of financing in the  constitution. They say it's because of historical
reasons. That's BS. When you do the constitution,  you redo the history. You start from scratch.
Because people were scared of this terrorist  movement, they were allowed the following bizarre
exception. Everybody gets financing through the  taxation system, and you get some taxes that go to
your region and some taxes that go to the central  government, except the Basque Country, which
has itself collects all the  taxes and negotiates bilaterally.
Imagine Texas negotiating bilaterally  with the US government, how much Texas
is going to contribute to the US budget. Now,  here's the smart thing, or the terrible thing.
They have enough votes to flip government  every few years. They wait for that negotiation
till the moment when they actually can decide  that this government is going to continue,
is going to drop. They do always the negotiation  in that moment, which means that what is called
the cupo, the contribution of the Basque Country  to Spain, is basically frozen. In fact, even
when the pensions go up, the rest of the country  pays them. The Basques don't actually pay more.
They actually are net recipients from Spain,  even though they are one of the richest regions.
Catalonia sees this and says, hey, we  want the same system. The problem is,
the Basque Country is small. Catalonia is very  large. It's not sustainable to do a system
like that because it would break the budget if  you have two of the biggest regions bargaining
bilaterally with the state over how much they're  going to contribute every five or 10 years.
That's going to be unsustainable. That's the  reason this basic inequality in the constitution
has created a system that is unstable, and  that doesn't actually have any solution at all.
COWEN: What did the University of  Chicago teach you about politics
that Spain ended up proving wrong?
GARICANO: I think what I learned  at the University of Chicago
helps very much with understanding politics.  Politicians are pretty smart maximizers.
I guess voters are pretty inattentive. I  think that your colleague, Bryan Caplan,
wrote a beautiful book about it, The Myth of the  Rational Voter, which is perfectly rational that
they are inattentive. If we doubt why do they  have the incentive to stand up and vote, why
would they have the incentive to figure out what  the program of the different parties is? They’re
inattentive. I think that that’s not clear enough  from the rational models of political economy.
The thing that I think I understood when I was  actually doing politics better than I understood
before, and I actually wrote a paper about  it, is the importance of the party discipline.
The mechanism that connects the voters to the  politicians is very weak because we have in many
countries in Europe, even in other countries,  happens through other means like in the UK, but
we don’t need to discuss that, but that mechanism  that connects the voters and the parties is a
mechanism that is mediated. Sorry, the voters and  the law is mediated by internal party discipline.
The parties don’t look for the smartest person  for the job or the most competent person for
the job or the person who can design the  right policy. They actually want people
who owe their position to the party so they won’t  complain. It’s not the one who in the town hall
votes more smartly or proposes the smartest things  who gets to the next layer of the proportional
representation system. It’s the one who’s  been most subordinate to the party decisions.
That’s why the Socialist Party, which is now in  enormous corruption scandals, unprecedented in
all directions, there is nobody in the party, and  definitely nobody in the Congress supportive of
Prime Minister Sánchez, who is actually making any  noise because their alternative option is zero.
The parties look for people whose outside option  is zero in order to make sure that they keep the
control. That’s, I think, completely rational,  and it would have been predicted by any Chicago
economist on the basis of the incentives, but  it’s not something that I was as aware of.
For example, how do parties in Europe choose  the president of the European Commission? Do
they choose the smartest person that  is going to make the best calls? No.
The leaders of the different countries, they  actually want to keep the power. They don’t want
somebody in Brussels who is kind of shallowing  them. They look for somebody who won’t give them
any trouble. We’ve had two Luxembourg people,  one failed defense minister from Germany who is
the current president. We have people who are  just not able to lead, and that is by design.
I think that part of how the party  machines and the insight of the way
that this promotion, adverse election, you could  say, this promotion to higher office gets done,
was something that I didn’t understand well  before politics, I think, not sufficiently well.
COWEN: You’ve served in the  European Parliament. Should
the EU keep its unanimity  rule for major decisions?
GARICANO: The EU has majority rule in  single-market decisions and unanimity rules
in things that fall out of its core, meaning  taxes, defense, foreign policy; in a sense,
you could say all the core functions of the state.  The states don’t want to lose decisions here.
Let me give you an example. Armament procurement.  You would say, “Hey, guys, you’re making multiple
tanks. You spend many times more in defense  than Russia. Just make one tank, make one plane,
and one cannon.” What happens? Well, let’s say  that Germany wants to export to Israel. France
doesn’t want that, let’s say, or Spain  doesn’t want that. Germany doesn’t want
Spain and France to make a coalition and  veto it, and vice versa. What happens is
the countries want to have the ultimate right to  decide on all defense matters. That means that you
get multiple procurement decisions, incompatible  shells in the cannons, all of these things.
Now, should we have it? Yes. Should we have  the majority vote that you proposed? Yes.
Should we understand the politics that  make it very hard? Those politics are
the core of the state sovereignty, which is  taxation, defense, foreign affairs, all this.
The functions that the state of 1600 or  1700 had originally are all not in Europe.
The politics make it very hard. I told you  defense, but I could go through many other
examples and show you why even though you would  want to think that the gains from a single market,
single procurement, et cetera, would be  enormous, the politics make it really hard.
Right now, what we’re doing is harmonizing the  shells. You have a big meeting group. People,
they say, “Oh, I want the 55 millimeters  to be like this.” Somebody says, “No,
I want it like this, 55 1/2.” They meet  for weeks and weeks and weeks and weeks
and come up with pages and pages. People, the  citizens are upset. The truth of the matter is
there is a political reason for  this, and it’s the one I mentioned.
So fiscal—Ireland wants to do a separate  tax in Luxembourg, separate tax policy
that basically attracts multinationals and  lowers the tax base and all of those things.
The rest would want no arbitration tax basis. This  is by unanimity. As long as there’s one loser,
no change takes place. In all of these  policies, there’s always one loser.
Pareto improvements are the  only ones that can happen.
COWEN: You have your finger on a button, and you  can press the button, and the unanimity rule goes
away, and it’s replaced by two-thirds  majority rule. Do you press the button?
GARICANO: Everything. Not  even the US has that, right?
COWEN: Correct.
GARICANO: Not even the US. Let’s say Europe gets  the same commerce clause as the US. Let me put it
like this. On the function that the US government  has, Europe loses unanimity, I would say yes.
COWEN: Could a euro bond work at a  significant level under current institutions?
GARICANO: No. You cannot have the four housemates  of the apartment share the credit card bill
without sharing anything about how the money  is spent and how the money is raised. Then
the incentives are for all the housemates to go  around with the common credit card and spend it.
I’ve been a very big proponent, and I was a  proponent of the recovery and reconstruction
fund for Europe. We proposed it together with some  revenue functions for Europe that would allow for
the Hamiltonian compromise. The money  gets centralized for some public goods
that are European public goods, and you raise  it in some European way. That has not happened.
We issued those bonds, which we do have, so euro  bonds do exist, without really any joint revenue.
COWEN: Capital markets seem to be a big problem.
What could we do to make EU capital  markets stronger and better?
GARICANO: It’s very interesting because I wrote  about this in Silicon Continent, in my Substack,
a piece with Per Strömberg. Sweden  has enough money to fund startups
and scale those startups up. Per Strömberg is one  of the biggest world experts on private equity,
and he happens to be also an expert in Sweden  because he’s based in the Stockholm School.
The basic story that he tells, and that I wanted  to write in a blog for our readers with him,
is that it is not really about having the cash.  It’s about the cash and the knowledge together.
The money exists. Europe sends the money to the  US. We invest in all those startups. The talent
exists; all those French and Germans in Anthropic  and all these other places. What is missing is
the Spotify chief of marketing that actually  has seen how companies run, how it’s scaled,
et cetera, and now has a lot of money, and starts  to fund startups, advise them, and help them.
It’s possible that it is true our capital markets  are a problem, but it is possible that just
fixing the other aspects, which is at the national  level allowing for the big change that Sweden did,
is that you don’t pay those taxes on the capital  gains as long as they are reinvested in the new
startups. Then you create this ball that starts  rolling in which all these startup funders start
funding the new startups. You can do it in a  country that was supposed to be one of the most
socialist in Europe. In fact, it’s a very  free market thanks to internal reform.
It’s true the capital markets are not working.  It’s also true the capital market changes we’re
doing are wrong. The main thing I learned about  Europe in that respect is when we do efforts,
instead of we put this new law and eliminate  the previous ones, the way it often happens
in the European Parliament, European Commission,  European Council, the European institutions, is
we add this new law which is harmonized,  but leave all the lower-layer laws there.
For example, we are giving right now in  the new capital markets package more power
to the European Securities Markets Authority,  the ESMA, the SEC at the European level,
without removing any power from the  SEC at the national level, which means
you’re not harmonizing anything. You’re just  having more hurdles for people to raise money.
COWEN: You mentioned your Substack,  Silicon Continent. I’m happy to recommend
that strongly as well. Now, in labor  markets, should severance protection
rise with the tenure of the worker, or  why not just let the market handle that?
GARICANO: I have written and argued  in favor of more flexible markets.
Denmark has found a solution that I think  achieves both ends in protecting workers by
having relatively or pretty high unemployment  insurance, but in making it flexible and able
to hire and fire. That would be, to me, the best  solution to the current rigidity on European labor
markets. The problem is that it costs quite a  bit of money because you have to insure people
quite significantly to make  them be happy to move around.
There are solutions in Northern Europe  that allow for this flexicurity, and
I would wish that the rest of Europe was adopting  them because I do believe that it’s not just that
rigid labor markets raise the cost for companies.  You can then lower wages and neutralize it.
The problem is they increase, hugely,  the cost of making mistakes. That’s what
a new literature is recognizing.  People weren’t clear about that before.
If Facebook makes a mistake, thinks the future is  the metaverse, and the metaverse is a completely
ridiculous idea, and the future is AI, Facebook  can turn on a dime, fire all the engineers in
metaverse, and hire all the ones in AI in a week.  If Ericsson or Nokia want to do something similar,
they’re going to take months and months and months  of negotiation with their labor council and so on
to the point that they might  go under in the meantime.

COWEN: Now, I agree with you, but I think my worry  is the opposite, that I know a lot of people,

and that if most jobs become messy jobs,
for them, that’s quite stressful, and they’re  upset and disoriented. Do you worry about that?
GARICANO: I think that we will have to have  a tolerance for human relations. Is that what
your friends don’t want? We have a tolerance for  relational work that is complex, that has politics
in it, that has a big human component, and  that’s the part that is going to stay. If people
just want to be in their desk typing away, I  think two good ways to think about it is work
from home and outsourcing. If you think of which  jobs were offshored, let me say offshored, in the
big offshoring wave to India, those are jobs  that are not messy. They’re clean. The company
specifies the jobs. They say, “Okay, we can  specify this job perfectly. Let’s ship you up.”
Those jobs are the same exact  ones that are under complete
threat of disruption. A lot of the work from home,
when it doesn’t involve a lot of submittings,  I guess, has the same feature. Those jobs are
clean, single-task, and very often verifiable.  You can just see how the performance is going
and have your RL, your reinforcement learning  loop work on those. I think those are gone.
The messy component that I want to  emphasize, many people will say, “Oh,
AI will tend to the messiness as well.” I think  that there is some messiness that is contingent

The favorite middle-of-the-road free market  economist prescription for technological change is

a clinician, a doctor who’s  learned to diagnose illnesses,
and that suddenly gets very easy—this  is not one of our examples, but just to
give an example—to become a plumber. It’s  not that you couldn’t retrain him because
the plumbing skills are so hard, which they  probably are, to be honest, but not just that, but
because there’s a lot of social identity and other  aspects that are tied to the kind of job you do.

is by dying, and the new generations do new  things. I share your concern about how easy
it will be to get people to learn new tricks. On  the other hand, my Ma is 84 years old, and she
talks to ChatGPT all the time. She has good, long  conversations. I’ve updated it so that she now has
